{{nihongo|'''Shirayama Hime Shrine'''|白山比咩神社}} is a [[shinto shrine]] in the [[Engishiki Jinmyōchō]]. It is located in [[Kaga Province]].

'''Shirayamahime Shrine''' (しらやまひめじんじゃ) is a {{jalink|Shinto shrine|Q845945}} located in Sannomiya-machi, {{jalink|Hakusan City|Q696407}}, {{jalink|Ishikawa Prefecture|Q131281}}. It is a {{jalink|Shikinaisha}}, the {{jalink|Ichinomiya|Q1656379}} of {{jalink|Kaga Province|Q907469}}. Under the {{jalink|modern shrine ranking system|Q712534|former shrine rank}}, it was a {{jalink|Kokuhei Chūsha}}, and today it is listed as a {{jalink|Beppyo Shrine|Q10898274}} of the {{jalink|Association of Shinto Shrines|Q908077}}.

It is the head shrine of more than 2,000 {{jalink|Hakusan Shrines|Q11579587}} nationwide. It is also commonly called “Shirayama-san,” “{{jalink|Hakusan Gongen|Q11579578}},” “Kaga Ichinomiya,” and “Hakusan Hongū.” Its {{jalink|shrine crest}} is the “Mitsuko-mochi Kikkō Urihana.”

=== Overview ===
The shrine stands at the foot of {{jalink|Mount Hakusan|Q2639098}} (2,702 m), which lies on the border of {{jalink|Ishikawa Prefecture|Q131281}}, {{jalink|Fukui Prefecture|Q133879}}, and {{jalink|Gifu Prefecture|Q131277}}, and enshrines Mount Hakusan as a {{jalink|sacred mountain|Q1595289}}.

Originally, the shrine was located at what is now Furu-miya Park by the {{jalink|Tedori River|Q11496932}}, but it was destroyed by fire in the {{jalink|Muromachi period|Q334845}} and relocated to its present site. There is also an {{jalink|inner shrine|Q11445659}} on the summit of Mount Hakusan at Gozenmine. The shrine at the foot of the mountain was therefore called “Lower Hakusan” or “Hakusan Hongū.”

Within the precincts are many cultural treasures, including a {{jalink|National Treasure|Q1139795}} {{jalink|sword|Q12791}} (signed {{jalink|Awataguchi Yoshimitsu|Q11604625|Yoshimitsu}}), as well as numerous {{jalink|Important Cultural Properties|Q1188622}}.

=== Enshrined Deities ===
The three principal deities are:
* '''Shirayamahime Ōkami''' — identified with {{jalink|Kukuri-hime no Kami|Q11619891}}.
* '''{{jalink|Izanagi|Q813858|Izanagi-no-Mikoto}}'''
* '''{{jalink|Izanami|Q682306|Izanami-no-Mikoto}}'''

=== History ===

=== Historical Overview ===
{{main|Hakusan Faith}}
Mount Hakusan is counted among the {{jalink|Three Sacred Mountains of Japan|Q11086198}} and has been revered since ancient times. According to shrine tradition, a ritual site for distant worship of Hakusan was established during the reign of {{jalink|Emperor Sujin|Q333530}}. In the 2nd year of {{jalink|Reiki|Q1373115}} ({{jalink|716|Q23531}}), the shrine was relocated to Yasutō no Mori and shrine buildings were erected.

In {{jalink|717|Q23532}}, the ascetic monk {{jalink|Taichō|Q2388439}} climbed Mount Hakusan and founded it as a sacred mountain. An inner shrine was established on the main peak, Gozenmine, and {{jalink|Hakusan Gongen|Q11579578|Hakusan Myōri Daigongen}} was enshrined.

The earliest reliable historical record states that Shirayamahime-no-Kami was granted the rank of Junior Third Rank in {{jalink|853|Q30367}}.

Thereafter, the shrine was designated the Ichinomiya of Kaga Province and flourished for roughly 500 years from the mid-{{jalink|Heian period|Q193292}} through the {{jalink|Kamakura period|Q236205}} and into the early {{jalink|Muromachi period|Q334845}}.

It was also a major center of the {{jalink|Hakusan Faith|Q11579557}} and the {{jalink|Zenjōdō|Q11591175}} pilgrimage routes, alongside Echizen Baba ({{jalink|Heisenji Hakusan Shrine|Q11483206}}) and Mino Baba ({{jalink|Nagataki Hakusan Shrine|Q11653351}}). Through rights related to managing the mountain and collecting pilgrimage fees, it prospered.

However, from {{jalink|1455|Q6480}} onward, the spread of the {{jalink|Kaga Ikkō-ikki|Q20982977}} led to financial hardship, and in {{jalink|1480|Q6628}} a great fire destroyed the shrine. The site of Sannomiya was designated as the new location in {{jalink|1488|Q4853}}.

The shrine was rebuilt in {{jalink|1596|Q6785}} under {{jalink|Maeda Toshiie|Q1196817}} after receiving an imperial edict, and during the {{jalink|Edo period|Q184963}} it was supported by the lords of the Kaga Domain.

After the {{jalink|Meiji period|Q3125096}} {{jalink|Shinto-Buddhist separation|Q1970535}}, the shrine took its present name, Shirayamahime Shrine. Following World War II, it became a {{jalink|Beppyo Shrine|Q10898274}} of the {{jalink|Association of Shinto Shrines|Q908077}} and was granted stewardship over approximately 3,000 hectares surrounding the summit of Mount Hakusan.

In the 42nd year of {{jalink|Meiji|Q3125096}} ({{jalink|1909|Q2057}}), on July 23, the 2,000th Anniversary Grand Sengu Festival (Shikinen Taishō) was conducted. In the 33rd year of {{jalink|Shōwa|Q327567}} ({{jalink|1958|Q5253}}), on October 3, the 2,050th Anniversary Grand Sengu Festival was conducted. In the 55th year of {{jalink|Shōwa|Q327567}} ({{jalink|1980|Q2439}}), on October 3, the 500th Anniversary Grand Sengu Festival commemorating the transfer of the main sanctuary from the former shrine site to the site of Sannomiya was conducted. In the 20th year of {{jalink|Heisei|Q234510}} ({{jalink|2008|Q2004}}), on October 7, the 2,100th Anniversary Grand Sengu Festival was conducted.

In Heisei 29 ({{jalink|2017|Q25290}}), the Grand Commemorative Festival Celebrating the 1,300th Anniversary of the Opening of Mount Hakusan by Taichō (August 9–11) was held.<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.shirayama.or.jp/topics/h29/t2913.html#t|title=紡がれた悠久の時を寿ぐ 白山開山1300年記念奉祝大祭のお知らせ|work=|publisher=Hakusan Hime Shrine Official Website|accessdate=2017-8-10}}</ref>

=== The Origins of the Deity Hakusan Hime ===
Rising white and shining above blue-hazed mountain ranges seen from the wide plains, Mount Hakusan has since ancient times been revered from afar as a mountain enshrined as a {{jalink|shintai|Q327532|sacred mountain}}—a deity of water blessings essential to agriculture—and is said to have served as a “mountain marker”<ref group="注釈">A landmark used to determine position at sea; see the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism, Urban and Regional Development Bureau, Remote Islands Promotion Division explanatory page “Mountain-Mark Islands.”</ref> for offshore fishing and navigation.<ref group="注釈">From shrine tradition and oral histories of fisheries cooperatives supporting the Mienie-kō.</ref>

According to shrine tradition, the founding dates to the mythological era, close to the reign of {{jalink|Emperor Sujin|Q333530}}, year 7 (91 BCE), when a {{jalink|himorogi|Q60587|sacred ritual enclosure}} was established on Mount Funao.<ref group="注釈">See the “Ishikawa New Information Repository” website.</ref> In the 28th year of {{jalink|Emperor Ōjin|Q317997}} ({{jalink|297|Q33553}}), it was moved down to Jūhachi-kōgawara,<ref group="注釈">A location near the right bank of the Tedori River close to the foothills of Mount Funao.</ref> and is said to have been repeatedly washed away by floods. In the 2nd year of {{jalink|Reiki|Q1373115}} ({{jalink|716|Q23531}}), by imperial command under {{jalink|Empress Genshō|Q235343}}, it was relocated to the higher forest of Akutō and shrine buildings were constructed.<ref group="注釈">See “Hakusan no Ki.”</ref> In the first year of {{jalink|Kashō|Q1373157}} ({{jalink|848|Q30380}}), it is said that 45 shrine and temple buildings were completed.<ref group="注釈">See “Hakusan no Ki” ({{jalink|1163|Q19672}}).</ref>

In the {{jalink|Heian period|Q193292}}, the shrine appears at the head of the ten shrines of {{jalink|Ishikawa District, Kaga Province|Q1155548|Ishikawa District}} in the {{jalink|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|Q11064932}}.

The earliest reliable documentary reference records that Hakusan Hime was first granted the rank of Junior Third Rank in the 3rd year of {{jalink|Ninju|Q1373077}} ({{jalink|853|Q30367}}).<ref name="文徳五" group="注釈">{{jalink|Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku|Q1052905}} vol. 5; and {{jalink|Ruijū Kokushi|Q1038639}} vol. 14.</ref> On the 27th day of the first month of the first year of {{jalink|Jōgan|Q1075635}} ({{jalink|859|Q23897}}), it was promoted to Senior Third Rank.<ref group="注釈">{{jalink|Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku|Q1052981}}.</ref> During the Heian period, it received imperial treasure and offering envoys as one of the deities of the Seven Circuits of the Capital region.<ref group="注釈">{{jalink|Sakyōki|Q11479706}}.</ref>

According to the shrine chronicle “Hakusan no Ki” (also called “Hakusan Engi,” {{jalink|1163|Q19672}}), the inner torii was at Kashitaka (Tsurugi area), the second torii at Tsukihashi, and the main gate at Kōgo on the {{jalink|Hokurikudō|Q3139239}}, where travelers worshipped Mount Hakusan from afar and received talismans. It further states that in the 5th year of {{jalink|Chōwa|Q1194173}} ({{jalink|1016|Q19247}}), offerings from seven ports of Kaga Province began the Mienie-kō ritual praying for bountiful catches.

By the late Heian period, the shrine became the central institution of the Kaga Zenjō pilgrimage route and was designated the {{jalink|Ichinomiya|Q1656379}} of {{jalink|Kaga Province|Q907469}}, conducting official provincial rites to encourage agriculture. As Hakusan Hongū, its subsidiary and related shrines spread widely from Echigo to Noto and Kaga.

=== Shinbutsu-shūgō (Syncretism of Kami and Buddhas) ===
{{Main|Hakusan faith}}
From the mid-Heian period (around the 9th century), Buddhist theories such as {{jalink|honji suijaku|Q2279088}} emerged, asserting that kami were manifestations of buddhas. As {{jalink|Shugendō|Q1483875}} practitioners increased, choosing sacred mountains as training grounds under the influence of {{jalink|Tendai|Q668188}} and {{jalink|Shingon|Q550182}}, Mount Hakusan transformed from a nature-worshipped mountain into a syncretic sacred site of ascetic practice.

As bases for ascent to the {{jalink|summit of Mount Hakusan|Q2639098}}, the Kaga, Echizen, and Mino pilgrimage routes were established around the 9th year of {{jalink|Tenchō|Q1373138}} ({{jalink|832|Q23900}}). Hakusan Hongū flourished for about 500 years from the mid-Heian through early Muromachi periods.

In the 3rd year of {{jalink|Kyūan|Q1193860}} ({{jalink|1147|Q19629}}), {{jalink|Heisenji Hakusan Shrine|Q11483206}} became affiliated with {{jalink|Enryaku-ji|Q917195}}, and Hakusan Hongū formed the {{jalink|Seven Shrines of Hakusan|Q11579548}}.

According to various texts, the monk {{jalink|Taichō|Q2388439}} of Echizen, through ascetic practice, perceived the manifestation of {{jalink|Eleven-faced Kannon|Q11404731}} and opened Mount Hakusan, establishing the inner shrine on {{jalink|Mount Hakusan|Q2639098}}’s main peak.

=== Decline from Late Heian Prosperity to the Muromachi Period ===
From the mid-Heian through early Muromachi periods, the shrine prospered and was revered by eminent monks. In {{jalink|1177|Q19694}}, the Hakusan monks carried three mikoshi to {{jalink|Kyoto|Q740246}}, causing the {{jalink|Shishigatani Incident|Q73140}}.

However, from the mid-Muromachi period onward, the shrine declined due to the rise of warrior power and the spread of {{jalink|Ikkō-ikki|Q947533}} forces. In {{jalink|1480|Q6628}}, a great fire destroyed the shrine, and it remained in decline for over a century.

=== Edo Period Reconstruction and After ===
Reconstruction began under {{jalink|Maeda Toshiie|Q1196817}} following an imperial edict from {{jalink|Emperor Ōgimachi|Q334076}}, and was completed in {{jalink|1596|Q6785}}. During the Edo period, the Maeda lords managed the shrine, rebuilding its halls and associated temples.

=== Meiji Period and Beyond ===
During the {{jalink|Meiji Restoration|Q8707}}, the {{jalink|Shinbutsu bunri|Q1970535}} policy abolished syncretism. The shrine enshrined Shirayamahime Ōkami (identified with {{jalink|Kikuri-hime|Q11619891}}), {{jalink|Izanagi|Q813858}}, and {{jalink|Izanami|Q682306}}, restoring the ancient name Hakusan Hime Shrine and abolishing the associated temple.

After World War II, while other Hakusan shrines also claimed central status, Hakusan Hime Shrine became a {{jalink|Beppyo Shrine|Q10898274}} under the {{jalink|Association of Shinto Shrines|Q908077}}, receiving approximately 3,000 hectares around the summit as its precincts.

=== 2,100th Anniversary Grand Festival ===
From October 7, 2010, a five-day grand festival was held successfully, featuring traditional performances and nationwide participation, and discussions began on cooperative development among the three pilgrimage routes.
